source.title: The Rich and the Simple: On the Implicit Bias of Adam and SGD
source.authors: Bhavya Vasudeva; Jung Whan Lee; Vatsal Sharan; Mahdi Soltanolkotabi

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Compares Adam and SGD on held-out performance using different tasks and metrics from the optimizer comparisons in V4; it does not test memorization of random labels or the other mapped interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports optimizer comparisons on held-out accuracy and subgroup robustness. Its citations to prior work are not extracted as results. The batch-size-50 experiment reports a qualitative boundary comparison but no test-accuracy result, so it does not supply a row.
record.test_reason: The study explicitly qualifies the view that SGD generalizes better than Adam, using its own held-out accuracy comparisons. Its spurious-correlation settings and broader optimizer tuning bear on V4's scope, without reproducing its limited-tuning premise.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate: the authors find richer feature learning with Adam and benefits under selected spurious correlations and distribution shifts, while allowing simplicity bias to help in-distribution generalization. Their blanket claim of better average subgroup-benchmark accuracy needs qualification: Table 13 favors SGD on CelebA and CivilComments, and Table 14 shows a substantial CivilComments average-accuracy advantage for Adam rather than merely comparable performance.
record.recipe_differences: Compares Adam with SGD on synthetic and spurious-correlation tasks, including optimizer-specific hyperparameter sweeps and subgroup-robustness metrics; it does not reproduce the optimizer comparisons in V4.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and metric affect the comparison: Adam improves worst-group accuracy throughout the subgroup benchmarks, while average accuracy is lower on CelebA and CivilComments in the larger-batch results. For smaller batches, authors report smaller gains on image datasets and larger gains on language datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Dominoes decoded worst-group accuracy improves after balanced last-layer retraining; Boolean decoded correlations likewise show more recoverable core information with Adam.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adam can learn representations containing more recoverable core-feature information than SGD in spurious-correlation tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Theory and decision-boundary plots distinguish simple GD features from richer Adam features, including a qualitative batch-size-50 comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adam can resist simplicity bias more strongly than GD in the studied settings.

record.problems: The theoretical results rely on population data and linear loss in simplified settings, as the authors acknowledge. The empirical results focus on spurious-feature tasks and subgroup robustness rather than ordinary in-distribution test error; the main comparison does not establish a training-test generalization gap. Optimizer-specific hyperparameters were swept for subgroup benchmarks.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result rows were omitted. The batch-size-50 Gaussian experiment in Section B.1 is not extracted because it reports qualitative decision-boundary differences, not a test-accuracy or generalization-gap value.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.

The original learning-rate-and-schedule-only tuning premise; the original benchmark comparisons; switching optimizers; decoupled weight decay; word-level language modeling. Equal training performance is not established for every comparison.
A controlled batch-size comparison with a documented common epoch budget. Tables 13 and 14 also change tuning recipes and do not isolate a batch-size penalty.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing memorized training examples and retraining.

missing.what: Gaussian held-out accuracy differences: Adam exceeds GD by 0.32, 0.595 and 0.203 percentage points in Section 4.1; by 0.618, 0.521 and 0.292 points in additional settings; and by 0.55 points for Figure 3. Preserve population versus finite-sample conditions and comparable-loss qualifications.

Additional original and core-only Dominoes accuracies: ResNet-18 at 99% correlation gives SGD/Adam 0.00/0.20 and 0.00/0.41; ResNet-34 gives 0.16/0.08 and 0.00/3.32 at 99%, and 0.24/9.60 and 0.00/18.31 at 95%. Include reported uncertainty. These expose conditions where Adam's absolute robustness remains very poor.

Boolean test accuracy across omitted initializations at matched loss: SGD/Adam 95.61/97.29, 95.00/98.13 and 96.08/97.77. Final accuracies across four initializations are 95.54/99.01, 94.96/99.28, 96.12/99.20 and 89.54/99.22. With nine core features, matched-loss accuracy is 83.47/94.22. Include uncertainty and endpoint distinctions.

record.verdict_notes: States use V4's usual Adam-worse direction; its broader-tuning qualification informs the verdict labels. Comparator states describe their paired optimizer comparison. Reported uncertainties do not by themselves establish significance. The study is not an original source for V4. No result directly challenges its specifically limited-tuning premise.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label memorization or natural-label held-out accuracy comparison of the same models.
No width sweep past the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.

Does not test limited learning-rate and decay-only tuning on the benchmarks in V4, or the cited language-model setting. Its reported comparisons include optimizer-specific hyperparameter sweeps and subgroup-robustness metrics.
No held-out performance comparison across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets; batch size 50 is used for a qualitative boundary comparison only.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization-gap comparison.
